response.text:
Assume \(m_1\) is the full model

\[
Y=\text{kid's IQ},\qquad X_1=\text{mom's IQ},\qquad X_2=\text{mom's age},
\]

\[
m_1:\quad Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{1i}+\beta_2X_{2i}+\varepsilon_i.
\]

### (1) Sample size

Residual df for \(m_1\) is \(431\). Since the model has 3 parameters \((\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2)\),

\[
n-3=431 \implies n=434.
\]

\[
\boxed{n=434}
\]

---

### (2) Fitted model \(m_1\)

\[
\boxed{\widehat{Y}=17.596+0.604X_1+0.388X_2}
\]

That is,

\[
\widehat{\text{kid IQ}}
=
17.596+0.604(\text{mom IQ})+0.388(\text{mom age}).
\]

---

### (3) LS estimate of \(\beta_1\) and interpretation

\[
\boxed{\hat\beta_1=0.604}
\]

Interpretation: holding mother’s age fixed, a 1-point increase in mother’s IQ is associated with an estimated increase of about \(0.604\) points in the child’s IQ.

---

### (4) Test \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) at 5%

Test statistic:

\[
t=\frac{\hat\beta_1-0}{SE(\hat\beta_1)}
=
\frac{0.604}{0.0587}
\approx 10.29.
\]

Degrees of freedom: \(431\).

At level \(\alpha=0.05\), the critical value is approximately

\[
t_{0.975,431}\approx 1.96.
\]

Since

\[
|10.29|>1.96,
\]

we reject \(H_0\).

Equivalently, the p-value is extremely small, \(p<2.2\times 10^{-16}\).

\[
\boxed{\text{Reject }H_0. \text{ Mom's IQ is a significant predictor of kid's IQ controlling for mom's age.}}
\]

---

### (5) Overall \(F\)-statistic for \(m_1\)

The overall model test is

\[
H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=0
\]

versus

\[
H_1:\text{at least one of }\beta_1,\beta_2\neq 0.
\]

Using

\[
F=\frac{R^2/p}{(1-R^2)/(n-p-1)},
\]

where \(p=2\) predictors, \(R^2=0.2036\), and \(n-p-1=431\),

\[
F
=
\frac{0.2036/2}{(1-0.2036)/431}
=
\frac{0.1018}{0.7964/431}
\approx 55.1.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{F\approx 55.1 \text{ on }(2,431)\text{ df}}
\]

with p-value essentially \(<2.2\times 10^{-16}\).

---

### (6) \(t\)-statistic for testing \(\beta_2=0\)

\[
t=\frac{\hat\beta_2}{SE(\hat\beta_2)}
=
\frac{0.388}{0.326}
\approx 1.19.
\]

\[
\boxed{t\approx 1.19}
\]

with \(431\) degrees of freedom. The corresponding two-sided p-value is about \(0.235\).

---

### (7) Hypotheses for the nested `anova(m2,m1)` test

Assuming \(m_2\) is the reduced model with mother’s IQ only,

\[
m_2:\quad Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{1i}+\varepsilon_i,
\]

and \(m_1\) is the full model with both \(X_1\) and \(X_2\), the nested ANOVA tests whether adding mother’s age significantly improves the model.

Thus

\[
H_0:\beta_2=0
\]

versus

\[
H_1:\beta_2\neq 0.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
H_0:\text{mom's age adds no explanatory power after controlling for mom's IQ}
\]

versus

\[
H_1:\text{mom's age adds explanatory power after controlling for mom's IQ}.
\]

---

### (8) Blanked ANOVA quantities and conclusion

For the nested comparison, the extra-sum-of-squares \(F\)-test has

\[
F=t_{\beta_2}^2\approx (1.19)^2\approx 1.42.
\]

The numerator df is the number of added predictors:

\[
df_1=1,
\]

and the denominator df is the residual df of the full model:

\[
df_2=431.
\]

So the p-value is

\[
p=P(F_{1,431}\ge 1.42)\approx 0.235.
\]

Using the given residual standard error,

\[
MSE=(18.26)^2\approx 333.43,
\]

\[
RSS_{\text{full}}=431(333.43)\approx 143707.
\]

The extra sum of squares is approximately

\[
SS_{\text{added}}=F\cdot MSE\approx 1.42(333.43)\approx 472.
\]

So

\[
RSS_{\text{reduced}}\approx 143707+472=144179.
\]

Thus the nested ANOVA table entries are approximately

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
\text{Model} & \text{Res.Df} & RSS & Df & F & p\text{-value}\\
\hline
m_2 & 432 & 144179 &  &  &  \\
m_1 & 431 & 143707 & 1 & 1.42 & 0.235
\end{array}
\]

Conclusion:

\[
p\approx 0.235>0.05,
\]

so we fail to reject \(H_0\). There is not significant evidence at the 5% level that mother’s age improves prediction of kid’s IQ after accounting for mother’s IQ.
